annotations.text:
PICK A DIRECTION

Four genuinely different answers to the same brief, not four shades of one. Each column is one direction: the marketing home page on top, the in-game dashboard below it — because a direction can sing on a landing page and die under real data density.

Everything on these frames is real: Arsenal's colour, squad and stadium out of src/data/plTeams.js; the league slice, budget and gameweek are plausible mid-season sample values.

Same information architecture in all four, so you are judging LOOK AND FEEL, not structure:

· Home page IS the entry. One primary action — choose a club — with no sign-up wall in front of it. Returning players get 'continue' underneath.
· Five destinations: Home, Squad, Table, Market, Club. Play is not a nav slot — it lives on the card you are already looking at, one tap from landing.
· Nav is a flat bar, no floating action button, labels always visible.

These are static sketches. Once you pick one I build the full set as a working click-through: club select, squad, tactics, transfers, academy, trophies, settings, inbox and the five-beat match flow.

A · EDITORIAL

Broadsheet sports desk. Paper cream, ink black, one stamp red. Instrument Serif over Archivo, hard rules instead of cards, real whitespace.

FOR — Looks like nothing else in the category. Light-mode-first makes the marketing page feel like a proper website rather than a game menu. Ages well.

AGAINST — The quietest of the four. Little inherent drama for the live match, which will need its own darker treatment. Serif display needs care at small sizes.

B · ALMANAC

Sticker album. Warm cream, hard black keylines, offset shadow, teal and amber. Bricolage Grotesque over Hanken Grotesk. Tactile and collectible.

FOR — The friendliest by a distance, and the most likely to convert a casual visitor. Chunky geometry gives generous touch targets for free. Distinctive.

AGAINST — The heavy borders and shadows eat vertical space, which hurts on the dense screens — a 20-row league table or a 3,000-row transfer list has to shed the frame. Risks reading as childish to a hardcore manager player.

C · BOARDROOM

Swiss data instrument. Cool greys, hairline rules, one signal red, Chivo over IBM Plex Mono. Everything on a strict grid.

FOR — Handles density better than any other option: tables, the transfer market and the squad list are its home ground. Fast to scan. Cheapest to build well.

AGAINST — Very little warmth or occasion. Sells the spreadsheet, not the Saturday. Also the closest of the four to a generic dashboard, so it works hardest to feel like football.

D · FLOODLIGHT

Stadium at night. Green-black ground, sodium-lamp amber, Anton over Barlow, soft light bloom behind the type.

FOR — The most atmospheric, and the only one where the live match needs no separate mode — it is already matchday. Amber is unusual for football UI; the club colour still has room to sit beside it.

AGAINST — Dark UI is the category default, so it is the least differentiating overall. All-caps Anton is inflexible for long strings — club names like 'Wolverhampton Wanderers' will fight it.

HOW TO ANSWER

Just name a letter. If you want to mix — say, B's warmth with C's density on the data screens — say that too; these are not locked packages.

Worth deciding at the same time:

1. LIGHT OR DARK as the default. A, B and C are light-first; D is dark. A browser game shown to a stranger on a phone in daylight argues for light; a match at 11pm argues for dark. Whichever you pick, the other becomes the match-mode counterpart rather than a full second theme.

2. HOW LOUD THE CLUB COLOUR GETS. These frames use Arsenal red sparingly — crest and the your-row marker. Turning it up makes each career feel personal but costs the design its own identity, and 186 clubs includes white (Leeds, Fulham) and near-black (Newcastle), which need a contrast guard whatever we choose.
